title: Genesis 3:16–24
context: Pain in childbearing, a disordered desire and rule between wife and husband, a cursed ground, sweat, and dust-to-dust mortality: the LORD names what sin has done. Yet He clothes them with skins, and Eve is named mother of all living, before cherubim and a flaming sword bar the way to the tree of life. Genesis 3:16–24 is judgment with mercy in it—exile that both punishes and protects, while the promise of 3:15 still stands.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on pain, toil, clothing, and exile from the garden, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The beasts whose skins they were, must be slain; slain before their eyes to shew them what death is. Thus the first thing that died was a sacrifice, or Christ in a figure.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 3:21)

reformed.quote: Unto Adam also , and to his wife , did the Lord God make , etc. Moses here, in a homely style, declares that the Lord had undertaken the labor of making garments of skins for Adam and his wife. It is not indeed proper so to understand his words, as if God had been a furrier, or a servant to sew clothes.

verses.text: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. You will bear children in pain. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Pain is multiplied in childbearing; children will still come, but through pain. “Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” After the fall, the closest bond is disordered—not erased.

Wesleyan Arminians hear consequence, not a new creation ordinance of domination. This is what sin does to marriage; it is not a license for abuse. In Christ the curse-tinged rule is to be redeemed, not baptized as God’s ideal for husbands.
verses.reformedNotes:
The woman’s sentence is pain and a bent relationship: desire and rule now grate rather than serve. Both camps historically refuse to treat this as permission to harm.

Reformed readers often hear creation order intensified as judgment—headship was not invented here (2:18–24), but after the fall it is heavy. The LORD names a wound He did not author as sin, even as He remains Lord over the household that must now live east of innocence.

verses.text: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and have eaten from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.
verses.arminianNotes:
Adam is judged for listening to his wife and eating the forbidden tree. The ground is cursed because of him; in pain he will eat of it all his days. His listening was an unforced revolt.

The earth suffers because the image-bearer refused the word. Grace had given a clear command; the sentence answers that refusal, not an unseen decree that made eating inevitable. Adam is not a bystander in this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Because you have listened… and have eaten”: the covenant head is addressed, and the ground is cursed “is cursed for your sake. You.” Romans 5 will make this representative: in Adam death spread to all.

God ordained to permit this without being the author of Adam’s sin. The field now fights the farmer because the representative fought his Maker. Judgment is personal and cosmic at once. Federal headship is already on the soil.

verses.text: It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.
verses.arminianNotes:
Thorns and thistles, yet still “the herb of the field.” The curse is no empty threat; so is remaining provision. Work is not abolished; it is made hard.

For the hearer: common kindness in a judged world invites gratitude and repentance, not presumption. The ground yields food enough to live and enough frustration to remember the fall. Mercy here does not cancel the need of the promised Seed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Thorns answer the man who reached for a tree. Yet he will eat. Mercy is stitched into judgment: the field still feeds, though it now resists.

This is common-grace provision under curse. God does not owe the rebel a harvest, and He still gives one. The world is not discarded; it is placed under a discipline that looks toward redemption.

verses.text: You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground, for you were taken out of it. For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Sweat, bread, return to the ground: dust to dust. Mortality is now the human story. The warning of 2:17 has arrived as a way of being, not only as a moment.

Classical Arminians take this as the grave consequence of a chosen revolt. Death is not a metaphor. The promise of 3:15 still sits over this dust—life will have to come as gift, received by faith, not as a right seized from the tree.
verses.reformedNotes:
Bread by sweat until dust returns to dust. The wages of sin are not delayed forever. Out of the ground he was taken; to it he goes.

Original guilt and corruption now have a cemetery. Federal death in Adam is as wide as the race. Even here the sentence is measured—he will eat until he returns, not be unmade on the spot. Common-grace mercy remains in the bread of the interval.

verses.text: The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man names his wife Eve, “because she would be the mother of all the living.” After dust-talk, he speaks life. The name leans on the promise just given.

This is faith’s instinct, not denial. If the Seed of the woman will bruise the serpent, motherhood is not futile. Hope names her against the grain of verse 19—and that hope is the gospel already offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Eve—“living”—is named under a death sentence. The line will continue because God said enmity and offspring, not because the pair can guarantee a future.

Providence keeps the mother of all the living in the story He will save. The name is a confession that life still belongs to the LORD who judged them. Shared ground: this is not cynicism; it is hope under sentence.

verses.text: The LORD God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD God makes garments of skins and clothes them. Fig leaves are replaced by a covering He provides. They do not dress themselves out of this shame.

Arminian readers see mercy that invites faith in the promised Seed. Do not over-claim a “first sacrifice” the text does not name; do claim a God who covers. The very Lord who sentenced them now stoops to clothe them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Skins instead of leaves: God covers what they cannot cover. Many Reformed readers hear a type of substitutionary covering—life given for a covering—while still refusing to force later ritual onto a verse that does not say “sacrifice.”

Clothing is grace in the midst of judgment. The Judge is also the dresser of Adam and Eve. What He provides is enough to walk east in, not enough to reopen the tree of life. Shared ground: this covering is gift.

verses.text: The LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever—”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” The seized likeness is tragic, not triumphant. The unfinished sentence—lest he also take of the tree of life and live forever—treats endless life in sin as a horror to be prevented.

Exile is judgment and protection. They chose revolt; they must not be immortalized in it. The barred tree is severe kindness, and 3:15 is still held out on the other side of the gate.
verses.reformedNotes:
The “us” of holy counsel names a knowledge now twisted by guilt. Living forever in that state would freeze rebellion. The LORD speaks a purpose before He acts.

God sovereignly bars the tree. This is not panic; it is mercy in judgment. The man who grabbed at divine prerogative will not also grab immortality on his own terms. Shared ground: exile keeps them from being sealed in sin.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken.
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore the LORD God sent him out to till the ground from which he was taken. Vocation continues east of Eden: the soil of his making is now the soil of his labor and his grave.

Classical Arminians hear an actual consequence of a chosen revolt. Sending is not theater. Yet the man is sent to work, not to nowhere—the promise of the Seed goes with a working, mortal pair who may still believe it.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Therefore” ties the expulsion to the danger of the tree of life. God sends; the man does not wander out on a whim. Work remains, now outside the garden.

God himself sends Adam out of the garden. The ground from which he was taken will occupy him until it receives him. Judgment assigns the task; providence still gives him a place to do it. Common-grace mercy: he is sent to work, not erased.

verses.text: So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.
verses.arminianNotes:
He drove out the man, and east of the garden He placed cherubim and a flaming sword turning every way to guard the way to the tree of life. Return on our terms is impossible.

This is the cost of the revolt they chose, and it is also protection from a cursed immortality. The way to life will have to be gift through the promised Seed, not a back door past the sword. The promise of 3:15 is still held out east of the gate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Drove out, placed, guarded: the verbs are God’s. Cherubim and a turning sword make the bar visible. No human hero will rush the tree.

The sovereign bar stands until God Himself opens a better way. The church later learns that way in the wounded Seed of 3:15. Mercy and judgment share this gate—life is not seized; it is given. Shared ground: exile is both sentence and shield.
